title: Why your brain keeps making you check your phone
description:
Why do you keep checking your phone when nothing new happened? Psychologists point to variable rewards: most checks give you nothing, some give you something good, and that unpredictability keeps the habit going.

Sources: Ferster & Skinner, 1957, Schedules of Reinforcement; Oulasvirta et al., 2012, Personal and Ubiquitous Computing ("Habits make smartphone use more compulsive").

#shorts #psychology #brain

scenes.headline: WHY?
scenes.text: Why can't you stop reaching for your phone when you know nothing is there?

scenes.headline: VARIABLE REWARD
scenes.text: Psychologists point to something called a variable reward.

scenes.headline: EACH CHECK
scenes.text: Most checks give you nothing. Some give you something good.

scenes.headline: CAN'T PREDICT
scenes.label: URGE
scenes.text: And that unpredictability is exactly what keeps animals pressing a lever in classic experiments.

scenes.headline: NEXT ONE MIGHT
scenes.text: Your brain learns that the next check might be the one.

scenes.headline: NO DECISION
scenes.text: So you reach, without deciding to.

scenes.headline: ONE STUDY
scenes.text: In one study of smartphone habits, checks were brief, repeated and often triggered by context cues.

scenes.headline: SO WHY?
scenes.text: So why can't you stop? Because the next one might pay off.
